Q: Why does Powershell combines array of arrays? A:

Some detailed tests reveal the following behaviour:

# array with single subarray - 1 top-level element
$array1 = @(
    @('element11','value11') # <-- $array1 (both elements)
) #    ^$array1[0] ^$array1[1]
echo $array1    # both elements
echo $array1[0] # 'element11' ------------> 1st array index level
echo $array1[1] # 'value11' --------------> 1st array index level

# array with comma and single subarray - 2 top-level elements
$array2 = @(,
    @('element21',  'value21') # <-- $array2[0] (both elements)
) #   ^$array2[0][0] ^$array2[0][1] 
echo $array2[0]    # both elements
echo $array2[0][0] # 'element21' ---------> 2nd array index level
echo $array2[0][1] # 'value21' -----------> 2nd array index level

# array with two subarrays - 2 top-level elements
$array3 = @(
    @('element31',   'value31'), # <-- $array3[0] (both elements)
  #    ^$array3[0][0] ^$array3[0][1]
    @('element32',   'value32')  # <-- $array3[1] (both elements)
) #    ^$array3[1][0] ^$array3[1][1] 
echo $array3       # all four elements
echo $array3[0]    # first two elements
echo $array3[0][0] # 'element31' ---------> 2nd array index level
echo $array3[0][1] # 'value31' -----------> 2nd array index level
echo $array3[1]    # second two elements
echo $array3[1][0] # 'element32' ---------> 2nd array index level
echo $array3[1][1] # 'value32' -----------> 2nd array index level

# array with comma then two subarrays - 3 top-level elements
$array4 = @(,
    @('element41',      'value41'), # <-- $array4[0][0] (both elements)
  #    ^$array4[0][0][0] ^$array4[0][0][1]
    @('element42',   'value42')    # <-- $array4[1] (both elements)
) #    ^$array4[1][0] ^$array4[1][1]
echo $array4          # subarray object 1, second two elements
echo $array4[0]       # first two elements
echo $array4[0][0]    # first two elements
echo $array4[0][0][0] # 'element41' ------> 3rd array index level
echo $array4[0][0][1] # 'value41' --------> 3rd array index level
echo $array4[1]       # second two elements
echo $array4[1][0]    # 'element42' ------> 2nd array index level
echo $array4[1][0][0] # 'e'     ^
echo $array4[1][0][1] #  'l'    |
echo $array4[1][0][7] #        '4'
echo $array4[1][1]    # 'value42' --------> 2nd array index level
echo $array4[1][1][3] #    'u'

i.e. it is not consistent.

Q: Why exit code 141 with grep -q? A:

No one canned reveal the topic)))

The problem is that files are streams and their internal descriptors are opened on them.
The data itself is read in batches.

In pipe, streams are implemented according to the operating principle of mkfifo `write => write lock => wait for read => Read`,

Example with mkfifo

rm /tmp/fifo_pipe
mkfifo /tmp/fifo_pipe
my_write()
{
     ping "google.com"  >> /tmp/fifo_pipe 
}

my_read(){
    while read -r line; do
        echo "Checked: $line"
        #rm /tmp/fifo_pipe
        return 0
        # or
        #exit 0
    done < "/tmp/fifo_pipe" 
}

my_write | my_read
echo $?

Error 141

This is explained by the fact that after reading the next packet in fifo_pipe, mkfifo starts the next recording process asynchronously, while the 2nd script processes the previous packet.

After recording, the first script stoped and wait for the second script to read it. After reading, the cycle repeats.

If the script is waiting to be read and completed, then naturally it will say - 141 error (Recording signal that the connection is broken)

The same thing will happen with the input stream.

 ping google.com | while read -r line; do
        echo "Checked: $line"
        exit 0
    done  
    echo $?

You can delete the file after reading (rm /tmp/fife_pipe) or close the input handle (exec 0>&-) but since the next write process has already occurred, somewhere in the back of your mind there is a checkmark `writted=1`

There are two possible solutions.
1. If the stream is a file, then at the end of pipe you just need to read it completely (...|cat <&0)
2. accept error 141 and the fact that the flow is interrupted

Q: Using rsync to delete a single file A:

You can use rsync for this, using the protect and risk filter flags. The idea is to sync an empty directory, but protect everything protect everything, except the single file of interest.

Assume you want to delete the file /path/to/file, then you can do the following:

$ mkdir /tmp/empty
$ rsync -avin --delete --filter 'risk /file' --filter 'protect /*' /tmp/empty/ user@host:/path/to/
